# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been marked by successive technological advances, from plain balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and subsequently drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. While modern DES have dramatically reduced restenosis and target-lesion revascularization, the permanent metallic scaffold remains a source of late adverse events, including neoatherosclerosis, chronic inflammation, and impaired vasomotion [2,3]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support during vessel healing and then fully resorb, theoretically restoring vascular physiology and eliminating the long-term risks of a permanent implant [4].

## Concept and Device Characteristics

The dominant BVS platform was the everolimus-eluting poly-L-lactide (PLLA) Absorb scaffold (Abbott Vascular), which received CE mark approval in 2011 [5]. PLLA degrades through hydrolysis into lactic acid, ultimately metabolized via the Krebs cycle, with complete resorption over approximately 2–3 years [6]. The proposed advantages included restoration of cyclic strain and vasomotion, late luminal enlargement, plaque regression, and freedom from the "metallic jacket" that complicates future surgical or percutaneous revascularization [7,8]. Magnesium-based scaffolds (Magmaris) offered an alternative metallic bioresorbable approach with faster degradation kinetics [9].

## Early Clinical Evidence

The ABSORB cohort studies provided proof of concept. ABSORB Cohort A demonstrated feasibility, while Cohort B showed durable results with evidence of restored vasomotion at long-term follow-up [10,11]. The ABSORB II randomized trial compared the scaffold with the Xience metallic DES and initially reported comparable angiographic and clinical outcomes at one year [12]. The pivotal ABSORB III trial randomized over 2,000 patients and met its primary noninferiority endpoint for target-lesion failure at one year, supporting U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval in 2016 [13].

## Emergence of Safety Concerns

Longer follow-up tempered initial enthusiasm. ABSORB II at three years revealed inferior late lumen dimensions and a higher rate of device thrombosis compared with Xience [14]. The ABSORB III trial at three years showed increased target-lesion failure and scaffold thrombosis, particularly in small vessels [15]. Meta-analyses pooling randomized trials consistently demonstrated an elevated risk of scaffold thrombosis, especially between one and three years—a period coinciding with scaffold resorption [16,17]. The AIDA trial reinforced these findings, reporting markedly higher definite or probable device thrombosis with Absorb [18].

Mechanistic explanations included the relatively thick struts (~150 µm) that disrupted laminar flow and delayed endothelialization, scaffold discontinuities during resorption, and acute recoil [19,20]. Intravascular imaging studies highlighted strut malapposition and uncovered struts as substrates for thrombosis [21]. These insights underscored the importance of meticulous implantation technique, leading to the "PSP" (pre-dilatation, sizing, post-dilatation) approach to optimize outcomes [22].

## Refinements and Subsequent Withdrawal

Registries employing optimized technique suggested that careful patient and lesion selection with proper implantation reduced adverse events [23]. Nonetheless, the cumulative evidence of harm prompted Abbott to withdraw Absorb from the commercial market in 2017 [24]. Long-term follow-up beyond three years offered some reassurance that the excess thrombosis risk attenuated after complete resorption, with later outcomes converging toward those of DES [25,26].

## Magnesium Scaffolds and Newer Platforms

The magnesium-based Magmaris scaffold demonstrated favorable results in the BIOSOLVE program, with low rates of thrombosis attributed to thinner struts and different degradation behavior [27]. Newer-generation bioresorbable devices with thinner struts, improved polymers, and enhanced radial strength are under investigation, aiming to overcome the limitations of first-generation technology [28]. Ongoing efforts focus on identifying populations—such as younger patients with large, non-calcified vessels—who might derive the greatest benefit from a transient implant [29].

## Conclusion

BVS represented an ambitious paradigm shift toward "leaving nothing behind" in coronary intervention. Although first-generation devices failed to demonstrate sustained noninferiority and were associated with increased scaffold thrombosis, the lessons learned have informed implantation technique, imaging-guided optimization, and device engineering [30]. The bioresorbable concept remains scientifically compelling, and refined next-generation platforms may yet fulfill its promise in carefully selected patients. Until robust long-term data confirm safety and efficacy, contemporary metallic DES remain the standard of care.
